xref.title: "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" Recording Location (April 1991)
xref.body: For the recording of "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," the Red Hot Chili Peppers moved into a historic mansion at 351 Laurel Canyon Boulevard, built in 1918. The house, with a reputation for being haunted and allegedly having secret tunnels to the nearby "Houdini Estate," was chosen by producer Rick Rubin for its isolated vibe. A Canadian company converted the basement into a recording studio. Chad Smith, however, was too unnerved by the house's atmosphere to stay there during sessions. "In April 1991, the Chili Peppers moved into a historic mansion at 351 Laurel Canyon, Boulevard that was built in 1918."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation of Pez - July 1993
xref.body: Ian received a phone call from Ben in July 1993, inviting him to start a new band with Ben, John, and Aaron. They held their first jam session in Ian's parents' basement that same month. "So our bands probably lasted a year each and then around July 1993. ... I got a phone call from Ben at one point and he was like me, Johnny and Aaron are thinking of starting a new band. Would you want to play with us? And so they all came over to my parents would let me jam in the basement. So they all came over and we had our first jam ever. Yeah. That was in July 1993."

xref.title: Formation and Early Cover Gigs (1996)
xref.body: The band started in 1996 in Colin McDonald's grandmother's basement, playing cover songs, including tracks by Tom Petty, The Beatles, The Tragically Hip, James Brown, and The Black Crowes. They gigged frequently in Antigonish high schools and local bars like Chuggles, Piper's Pub, and Pats Place, sometimes needing permission slips to play underage. "We started in 1996 and my grandmother's basement playing cover songs."

xref.title: "Civilianaires" Recording Departure
xref.body: The recording of the 2018 album "Civilianaires" marked a change in the band's approach. It was their first record that was not recorded "live off the floor," instead being built up track-by-track in producer Derek Hoffman's basement studio in Toronto. "That was the first time we made a record kind of not live off the floor."

xref.title: 606 East Studio in Virginia Basement
xref.body: Before the Foo Fighters established their dedicated 606 Studios in Northridge, California, Dave Grohl recorded a couple of the band's albums in his personal basement in Virginia. This informal recording space was affectionately referred to as "606 East." "606 East was Dave's basement in Virginia."

xref.body: Menza Droppo was the band Ash had started and was playing with when Jay first saw him perform in the basement of the Drake Hotel. Ash decided to revive this rock band in the past year. xref.title: Band Origins and Early Gigs
xref.body: The band was formed in Massachusetts in 1996. Their initial performances took place in the basement of a barber shop. They significantly developed their sound and presence after touring with The Mighty Mighty Bosstones, another band from the Boston area. "Their first gigs were in the basement of a barber shop, but after the muddy, muddy boss tones, another Boston area band, took them on tour, they really came into their own."

xref.title: Church Headquarters Acquisition - Farnham, Quebec
xref.body: Following the commercial success of *Funeral*, Arcade Fire invested in their future by purchasing an old building in Farnham, Quebec, about 70 kilometers southeast of Montreal. This building had previously served as a cafe (Petite Eglise) and a Masonic temple, and its basement was renovated into a recording studio. "They found this old place in Pharnam, Quebec, about 70 kilometers southeast of Montreal, and they turned it into a new headquarters."

xref.title: Drummer Booted
xref.body: Ben was "booted" from his drumming role in To Each His Own when Aaron Solowaniak, a more proficient drummer, was discovered practicing in a friend's basement. "And it was Aaron. And so I got the boot out of the band."

xref.title: Early Musical Development
xref.body: Avril Lavigne's musical talent was evident from an early age, starting with singing in church. Her parents fully supported her passion, providing her with musical gear and even building a small recording studio in their basement. "When she showed real talent, her parents went all in, not only providing her with gear, but also building a small recording studio in the basement."

xref.title: Early Rehearsals and Ramones Covers
xref.body: In their initial stages, Husker Dü honed their craft by playing covers of Ramones songs during rehearsals, often taking place in bassist Greg Norton's basement. This grounding in punk rock was combined with their later pop sensibilities. "And while the same time Husker Do was stumbling through remones covers during their first rehearsals and bassist Greg Norton's basement, another important Minneapolis band was coming together in a basement on Bryant Street South."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 8

xref.title: Early Songwriting Themes
xref.body: The Ramones began writing songs about what they knew, which largely involved being "near-to-wells" and "hoodlums" who were better at "hanging out, drinking, getting in fist fights, and doing drugs" than actual crime. Their early songs often began with the phrase "I don't want to," such as "I Don't Want To Get Involved With You," "I Don't Want To Walk Around With You," "I Don't Want To Be Learned, I Don't Want To Be Tamed," and "I Don't Want To Go Down To The Basement." "They started to write about what they knew, which was, well what exactly? Well, they were all a bunch of near-to-wells, a bunch of hoodlums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Studio in Mum's Basement
xref.body: With his brother Bob, Daniel Lanois established a studio in their mother's basement, where they assisted hundreds of local bands in recording demos. "Together with his brother Bob, they set up a studio in Mums Basements where they helped local bands record demos and apparently hundreds of groups made their way through that basement."

xref.title: Entry into Arkells and Professionalism
xref.body: Tim Oxford joined Arkells after attending audio school and networking through various pub gigs. He was introduced to the band by their previous keyboard player who mentioned they needed a drummer. His professionalism and working equipment (unlike the previous drummer's broken hi-hats) immediately impressed the band. He initially recorded a 5-song EP with them, some of which was done in his basement facilities. "Then when we met Tim, it was like, whoa, this guy is really professional because he was a very accomplished drummer, but his equipment also worked."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: First Gig at Erics Club (Year Unspecified)
xref.body: The band played their inaugural gig at Erics, a renowned basement club in Liverpool where many influential bands like The Clash, Sex Pistols, Devo, Pere Ubu, The Cure, and XTC performed. Erics had an open-door policy on Thursday nights, allowing unpaid members to showcase their music. "We used to go to a club in Liverpool called Erics, which was great. A very famous club."

xref.title: Formation Accident
xref.body: Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney, who met around ages 8 or 9 and became friends in high school in Akron, Ohio (both briefly attending the University of Akron), initially planned to record a demo for Dan's solo singer-songwriter pursuits. They invited musician friends to Patrick's basement, but on the appointed day in 2001, only Dan and Patrick appeared, leading them to spontaneously form a duo. "On the appointed day, no one except Dan and Patrick showed up. So that left the two of them to form a band on their own."

xref.title: Founding and Location
xref.body: Grant Avenue Studios is located in the east end of Hamilton, in a house originally built in 1917. Brothers Daniel and Bob Lanois established the studio here after moving their recording operations from their mother's basement laundry room. "When two Hamilton brothers, Daniel and Bob Landwaw, decided to move the recording business out of their mother's basement, they were set up in the laundry room, they moved into the house."

xref.title: Ian's Parents' Basement - Milk Crate Storage
xref.body: Ian D'Sa's parents' basement served as a storage location for the milk crates and plywood used for their DIY stages. At one point, there were approximately 500 milk crates stored there, causing the basement to reek of spoiled milk. "I remember one time there was like 500 milk crates in Ian's basement and his mom would come down and say, Ian, what are you doing with all these milk crates? Don't worry, mom, it's all good. Well, my parents' basement wreaked like, like, like, broad milk."

xref.title: Insane Family Life and Childhood
xref.body: His father, a religious extremist, threatened the family with death and dug graves in the basement of their New Hampshire log cabin to emphasize his seriousness. GG failed grade three, was bullied throughout school, and experimented with cross-dressing in high school. "Dad was a religious nut. He kept threatening the family with death. And to make sure they knew he was serious, he dug graves in the basement of their log cabin in New Hampshire. That's where you're gonna end up if you don't listen to me. Much insane family life ensued. GG failed grade three. He was bullied throughout school and experimented with cross dressing in high school."

xref.title: Killed in Richmond Spree Murders
xref.body: Brian Harvey and his family were among the victims of the Richmond Spree murders in January 2006, perpetrated by Ricky Gray, Ray Dandridge, and Ashley Baskerville. On January 1, 2006, police found Brian, his wife Kathy, their four-year-old daughter Ruby May, and nine-year-old daughter Stella Ann, bound and gagged in the basement of their burning house. Brian and Kathy had their throats cut and were bludgeoned with a claw hammer, Ruby was stabbed to death, and Stella Ann died of smoke inhalation. "First responders found Brian Harvey and his family, his wife Kathy, four-year-old daughter Ruby May, and non-year-old daughter Stella Ann, bound and gagged with packing tape in the basement of this house that was on fire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mother's Handmade Memorabilia for 606 Studios
xref.body: In a personal touch at Foo Fighters' 606 Studios, Dave Grohl's mother created throw pillows for the studio's couches using his old concert t-shirts. This memorabilia, alongside other Nirvana and Foo Fighters items, filled the building, much of which Dave previously stored in his mother's basement. "The most charming thing I saw were the throw pillows on the couches. They were made by Dave's mum from his old concert t-shirts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

xref.title: Nikolai Fraiture Backstage Incident
xref.body: During an early show where The Strokes opened for Girl Harbor at Don Hills, Nikolai Fraiture was caught having sex backstage in the basement and photographed. Girl Harbor then used this photo for a flyer for the next Strokes gig, with the caption, "this is what happened at our last show." "Nik was caught having sex backstage down on the basement and was photographed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producer of "Civilianaires"
xref.body: Derek Hoffman, a young producer based in Toronto, produced The Trews' 2018 album "Civilianaires." The album was recorded in his basement studio on the East End of Toronto, where tracks were built and vocals were layered, marking a sonic departure for the band. "He's a young, amazing producer from, well, he's in Toronto now."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

xref.title: Recording Studio in Church Basement
xref.body: The band transformed the basement of their purchased church in Farnham, Quebec, into a fully outfitted recording studio, providing them with a dedicated, cost-effective space to experiment and record without incurring large external studio bills. "The basement was renovated and outfitted with a recording studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Who the Hell is Arcade Fire? Part 1

xref.title: Rehearsal Space - The Shed
xref.body: After living in a friend's basement for a while, Isaac Brock built a shack next to his mother's trailer, which they named "the shed." This structure became the primary rehearsal space for Modest Mouse in their early days. "After living in a friend's basement for a while, Isaac built a shack next to the trailer and this became the rehearsal space for modest mouse. They called it the shed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Big Bands from Small Towns

xref.title: Resonance of "Tragically Hip" Lyric
xref.body: During a Saturday Night Live performance of "Grace, Too," Gord Downie became overwhelmed by the line "I'm tragically hip," which resonated so deeply with him that his "inner elevator went from the penthouse to the basement," causing him to forget the subsequent lyrics. "He said I'm tragically hip and it was like, because I just resonated with him and my inner elevator went from the penthouse to the basement. I'd break next speed and I thought I don't even know the next line."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Gord Downie: A Remembrance Part 2

xref.body: The Replacements, forming in a Minneapolis basement, honored their heroes, the Sex Pistols. They quickly became known for their unpredictable, high-energy performances in local clubs. "In honor of their heroes, the sex pistols, the replacements quickly became known for their unpredictable high-energy sets of clubs around town."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 8

xref.title: Shared Influences
xref.body: The two members, TheOGM and Yeti999, met by attending basement punk shows and shared a common appreciation for hardcore music, hip-hop, and horror movies, particularly those directed by Rob Zombie, which inspired their band's formation. "They met going to basement punk shows. They both loved hardcore and they loved hip-hop. They both loved horror movies, especially those directed by Rob Zombie, so why not form a band?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Black History Month 2023

xref.title: Van Theft & Polish Mafia (Poland)
xref.body: While on tour in Poland one Christmas, NoMeansNo had their rented van stolen after a show in Warsaw, containing about $10,000 worth of merchandise. With local police being unhelpful and the Dutch rental company concerned about insurance coverage outside Holland, a fan connected them with the Polish Mafia. Band member Rob Wright met two heavily armed men in a church basement and negotiated the van's return for 2000 German marks. The next day, the van and all its contents were recovered from a barn outside Warsaw. However, the Warsaw police later demanded another 2000 German marks for operating outside legal channels. "The next day the van was given the name of a village about 100 kilometers outside of Warsaw and told to wait in the town square."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
